The biggest single deal happened in April. Japan's MUFG Bank bought 20% of Shriram Finance for Rs 39,618 crore, about $4.4 billion. No foreign investor has ever put more into India's financial services sector in one deal.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 29%: Japan's share of the $19.81 billion India received that quarter
$4.4 billion: the MUFG deal, most of Japan's $5.71 billion
10 trillion yen: what Japan set out in 2025 to invest in India over 10 years

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Japanese companies are moving supply chains out of some countries because of political tension, tariffs and rising costs. Experts say these firms no longer see India only as a cheap place to make things. They also see a big market of buyers and a base for tech work. India wants this money. It has built 12 townships just for Japanese firms, with Japanese-standard utilities and help desks.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Experts say semiconductors, railways and defence are the likely next areas for Japanese money. Minister Piyush Goyal says Rs 1 lakh crore of the 10-trillion-yen pledge has already come in. But one bank deal can make a single quarter look huge. The real test is whether the money keeps coming.

recall.q: Japan was India's top FDI source in April to June 2026. What drove most of that money?
recall.a: One big financial deal, not new factories. MUFG Bank bought 20% of Shriram Finance for about $4.4 billion. That was most of Japan's $5.71 billion for the quarter.

cards.title: Being 'easy to get along with' can mean erasing yourself
cards.body: We praise people who are easy to please: the chill friend, the low-maintenance partner. But for one writer, being easy was not kindness. It was an old fear of conflict. Slowly, it wiped out her own wants, until her husband of four years did not know her favorite color.

sections.text:
Four years into their marriage, Dakota J. Dawson's husband turned to her in the car. He asked the kind of question people ask on a first date: what is your favorite color? She opened her mouth, and nothing came out. She was not hiding an answer. She could not find one that was truly hers.

Most of us think being easy to get along with is simply good. It keeps the peace, and it sounds generous. Dawson thought so too. A college roommate called her "so chill." A boyfriend told his mother she was low-maintenance. Each time, she felt proud, as if she had passed a test.

But being easy is not always a virtue. Sometimes it is a quiet way of erasing yourself.

Here is how it works. Anywhere is fine. You pick. I don't need anything. Said once, these words are polite. Said for years, they become reflexes: automatic answers that skip the real question of what you want. Dawson began to feel a small jolt of panic whenever a friend asked where to get coffee. She had stopped letting herself want things enough to name them. Her husband said it plainly. He used to think she was chill. Now he thought she was "really good at disappearing."

The reflex began in childhood. Her parents' moods could change a room in seconds. So she learned young to sense the mood and adjust before anyone asked. Agreeing felt safer than wanting, because wanting gave people something to say no to. That is the mechanism. Fear of conflict leads to self-abandonment, which means leaving your own needs behind to keep others calm. It was a survival skill that lasted long after the danger was gone. No one in her adult life asked her to be easy. Her husband and friends kept asking what she wanted. The fear was old, but the cost was real. By making herself so easy, she had made herself unknown.

Undoing it took tiny steps. She named an actual restaurant. She picked a different movie. She said no to hosting Thanksgiving. Her heart pounded every time, and every time the relationship held. Her favorite color, it turns out, is green, like the woods behind her childhood house.

So why does the myth survive? Because the praise feels so good. Being called easy sounds like proof that people want you around. But that praise rewards an edited version of you. And it hides what you gave up to earn it.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: You say 'whatever you want' before you have checked what you want.
You feel a small spike of fear when someone asks what you prefer, even about something tiny like coffee.
People close to you keep asking what you like, and you keep giving them no real answer.
Being called low-maintenance feels like the best compliment you could get.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one person's essay, not research. The link to her childhood is her own reading of her life. It is a strong example of the pattern, but it does not show how often the pattern happens or why.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The people who stayed were never staying for the easy version. They were staying for her.

recall.q: Why was being 'easy' not really a virtue for the writer, and where did the habit come from?
recall.a: Her constant 'anywhere is fine' was not generosity. It was a reflex that erased her own wants, so even her husband did not know her. It started in childhood. Her parents' moods could change quickly, so agreeing felt safer than wanting, because wanting gave people something to say no to.
